name: Egg oil skincare

lead: Egg oil is a lipid extract of hen egg yolk, rich in oleic and linoleic acids and phospholipids. People apply it as a moisturiser and conditioner for skin, aiming for softer, better-hydrated skin.

Traditional medicine systems used it for burns and dermatitis. Research includes a cell-culture study of a standardised egg oil and some animal work; human trials of its cosmetic effect have not been found.

paras: It is used as a topical oil or as an ingredient in creams, often at low concentrations in products. Patch testing is advised in the sources.

Residual egg proteins can cause contact dermatitis, hives or rarely anaphylaxis in people with egg allergy. Oils from unpasteurised yolk may carry Salmonella risk, the polyunsaturated fats oxidise over time, and heavy use may clog pores on acne-prone skin [1].

chain: Lipids form a barrier that reduces water loss
angle.text: Egg oil is applied as a moisturising, conditioning lipid. Its appearance effect is the barrier and softening action attributed to its fats.

lead: Egg oil is a golden-orange lipid extract from hen egg yolks containing triglycerides, phospholipids, cholesterol and unsaturated fatty acids such as oleic and linoleic acid [1]. People use it on skin as an emollient intended to soften and condition [1].

Historical sources describe egg yolk oil as a wound poultice in South Asian practice, a scalp treatment in Unani medicine, and a burn and dermatitis remedy in Traditional Chinese Medicine [1]. Egg yolk is also a source of lecithin and lutein [2].
A 2014 cell-culture study of a standardised egg oil (Charismon) reported effects on keratinocytes, immune cells and a human skin model after UV irradiation [3].

paras: Egg oil is made mainly by solvent extraction, with supercritical CO2 and enzymatic methods as alternatives [1]. Raw egg yolk is about 26.5 g fat per 100 g, mostly oleic (47%), palmitic (23%) and linoleic (16%) acids [2].
It is described as a moisturiser and skin conditioner; typical cream concentrations are given as 0.3-0.4% [1].

Egg allergy, Salmonella risk from unpasteurised yolk, oxidation of its fats and possible pore clogging are noted [1]. In the US it is a labelled cosmetic ingredient because eggs are a major allergen [1].

No studies found of egg oil in human skincare. Laboratory work on the standardised egg oil Charismon found that it stimulated IL-8 in keratinocytes, reduced several cytokines in activated lymphocytes, and strongly supported recovery of a skin model after UV exposure [3]. Rodent studies on burns and atopic dermatitis are described in a Grokipedia summary [1].
